statement: A strip has 4 squares in a row. Mia colours one or more squares so the strip looks the same when turned round flat, end to end. How many different strips can she make?

choices.misconception: I thought only colouring all 4 squares works.
I found the two end squares and the two middle squares but forgot colouring all four.
I also counted the strip with no squares coloured, but Mia colours at least one.
I counted every way to colour exactly 2 of the 4 squares, without checking the turn.

hints: When the strip turns round, where does the first square go?
Turning the strip end to end swaps the first square with the last, and the second with the third. So squares that swap must be coloured the same. Think of the strip as two pairs.
The end pair can be coloured or not, and the middle pair can be coloured or not. List the choices and remove the one where nothing is coloured.

solutions.reliable: Number the squares 1, 2, 3, 4. Turning the strip end to end puts square 1 where square 4 was, and square 2 where square 3 was. So squares 1 and 4 must match, and squares 2 and 3 must match. The choices are: colour the end pair only, colour the middle pair only, or colour both pairs. Colouring nothing is not allowed. That is 3 strips. The idea to keep: find which parts swap places, and colour each swapping group all the same.
solutions.elegant: Only two things are really chosen: the end pair (yes or no) and the middle pair (yes or no). That gives $2 \times 2 = 4$ ways, and one of them colours nothing, so $4 - 1 = 3$. The idea to keep: symmetry cuts a big count down to a few free choices.

whyOnTest: Symmetry turns four squares into two pairs, and the student who sees the pairs can list every strip in seconds.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
